paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process requires working with belief states, which represent uncertainty about the underlying state. These beliefs can occupy a very high-dimensional space, making optimal policy computation intractable. The paper addresses this obstacle by compressing beliefs into a smaller space where planning can be less expensive.

The proposed projection uses orthogonal non-negative matrix factorization. It seeks a compact representation that minimizes reconstruction error, while using orthogonality to make the compressed problem efficient to construct. The approach also incorporates the value function into the formulation: corresponding beliefs in the original and compressed spaces are intended to receive the same value under the stated construction.

This combination matters because faithfully reconstructing beliefs and preserving their planning values are distinct objectives. The method addresses both within its compression procedure. Tests on benchmark problems report substantial savings in the computational cost of finding policies, supporting the practical usefulness of the proposed representation for the evaluated planning problems.
icml-2007-a-novel-orthogonal-nmf-based-b.tldr: Orthogonal non-negative matrix factorization compresses POMDP beliefs while preserving corresponding values in its formulation and substantially reducing policy computation costs in benchmark tests.

paragraphs: The paper develops an inference algorithm for Dirichlet process mixture models, focusing on how to explore possible clusterings efficiently. Its motivation is that Gibbs sampling and variational approaches emphasize local changes. A method that can reconsider larger portions of a clustering may move more quickly through the space of possible solutions.

The key addition is an auxiliary permutation: an ordering of the data points that becomes part of the inference procedure. The sampler alternates between drawing a clustering and drawing an ordering. For a fixed ordering, dynamic programming makes it possible to consider all compatible clusterings, even though their number grows exponentially. Random projections provide an effective way to sample the orderings themselves.

The resulting procedure is described as stochastic hill climbing with more global moves. The reported benefit is significantly shorter burn-in than collapsed Gibbs sampling. This finding concerns how quickly the algorithm gets through its initial search phase; it supports the value of reorganizing the sampling problem around orderings and jointly considered clusterings.
icml-2007-a-permutation-augmented-sample.tldr: An auxiliary ordering lets a Dirichlet process mixture sampler consider large clustering changes efficiently and achieve substantially shorter burn-in than collapsed Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Mixture models can be trained to describe how data are distributed, but that objective does not directly prioritize classification. A density estimator tries to represent the distribution throughout the sample space. For classification, the density near the decision boundary is especially relevant because it helps determine which label an example receives.

The paper introduces a discriminative training method for mixtures of generative models. Its central computational move is to reduce training to fitting individual generative components on weighted data. This provides a way to pursue a classification-oriented objective through component learning, avoiding the demanding gradient search often used in discriminative mixture training.

That reduction matters particularly when each component is itself complex, such as a hidden Markov model or a Bayesian network. Such components can make direct gradient search difficult to use effectively. A comprehensive evaluation on time-series sequence classification demonstrates benefits of the proposed method, supporting its usefulness for classification problems where rich component models would otherwise make discriminative training costly.
icml-2007-a-recursive-method-for-discrim.tldr: The method trains discriminative mixtures through generative component learning on weighted data, making classification-oriented training efficient even with complex components.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether the promise of deep learning architectures extends to harder prediction problems. Its starting point is that impressive earlier results came from relatively simple settings, including digit recognition under controlled conditions. Those settings already allowed many learning algorithms to perform reasonably well, leaving a further question about the benefits of deeper models.

The authors conduct a series of experiments on problems with many factors of variation. The emphasis is on evaluating models when the data vary in more ways, rather than judging them only in controlled recognition settings. They compare deep architectures with established alternatives: support vector machines and feed-forward neural networks with a single hidden layer.

The experiments indicate that deep architectures show promise on these harder learning tasks. This is an empirical, qualified finding about their potential, rather than a claim that depth guarantees better performance. The contribution is to broaden the conditions under which these models are assessed and place their behavior alongside familiar classification approaches.
icml-2007-an-empirical-evaluation-of-dee.tldr: Experiments suggest that deep architectures are promising for harder problems with many factors of variation, compared with established classification methods.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing asks how a signal with many coordinates can be measured accurately using far fewer measurements. The paper presents this as a problem where machine-learning methods may contribute. The essential assumption is that the signal has a sparse representation in some basis, such as wavelets: relatively few coefficients are needed to express it.

The authors demonstrate how sparse Bayesian regression and active learning can be applied to this setting. Sparse regression connects the reconstruction problem to learning a compact coefficient representation. Active learning brings the question of choosing measurements into the same discussion, linking signal estimation with decisions about what information to collect.

The significance is the connection between a measurement problem and tools developed for learning from data. The ability to use fewer measurements rests on the stated sparse-representation assumption, rather than applying to arbitrary signals without structure. Alongside demonstrating these connections, the paper identifies further compressive-sensing research directions for the machine-learning community.
icml-2007-bayesian-compressive-sensing-a.tldr: The paper connects compressive sensing with sparse Bayesian regression and active learning under the assumption that signals have sparse representations.

paragraphs: Approximating a value function requires a representation that captures how useful different states are for decision making. Earlier graph-based approaches build basis functions from undirected connections between nearby sampled states. Their usefulness has been attributed to smoothness with respect to the geometry of the state space.

This paper investigates directed graphs, which can express the direction of state connectivity. That distinction matters for non-reversible Markov decision processes, where adjacent states may have substantially different values. The authors analyze the directed graph Laplacian through its Dirichlet sum, showing how the graph's invariant distribution affects the smoothness of the resulting basis functions.

The approach therefore connects approximation geometry with the directional structure of the decision process. It questions whether ordinary adjacency alone is the right guide for constructing smooth value representations. Experiments in both discrete and continuous problems with non-reversible actions report significant improvements in learned policies, supporting directed bases in the settings evaluated.
icml-2007-constructing-basis-functions-f.tldr: Directed graph bases account for non-reversible state connectivity and significantly improve learned policies in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: When a classification dataset contains unequal numbers of examples from different classes, many learning algorithms can lose performance. The paper studies whether changing the sample used for learning can help. Its contribution is a comprehensive experimental investigation of sampling for imbalanced data, organized around practical questions about when the intervention is useful.

The experiments consider more than whether sampling produces a single overall improvement. They ask whether its effectiveness depends on the kind of learner and whether conclusions change when a different performance metric is the objective. These questions connect the handling of class imbalance to both the learning algorithm and the way success is judged.

The main stated finding is that sampling improves classifier performance in many cases. That supports sampling as a potentially useful response to imbalance while preserving the qualification that the benefit is not universal. The experimental perspective matters because an assessment of sampling should account for the learner being trained and the performance objective being pursued.
icml-2007-experimental-perspectives-on-l.tldr: A broad experimental study finds that sampling improves classification on imbalanced data in many cases while examining learner and metric dependence.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process latent variable model represents high-dimensional observations through a lower-dimensional probabilistic description. This paper extends that approach by arranging the model into a hierarchy. The aim is to represent more of the organization within the data while retaining the ability to describe its lower-dimensional manifold structure.

A hierarchy, such as a tree, also expresses conditional independencies. In plain language, it can specify which parts of the data become independent once the relevant connecting variables are known. This adds a form of structural information to the representation: the model can describe both the shape of the data and how different parts depend on one another.

The authors first introduce Gaussian process hierarchies using a simple dynamical model. They then develop a more complex hierarchy and apply it to visualizing human motion datasets. The contribution is an extension of the modeling framework with an application showing how hierarchical latent structure can be used to organize and visualize high-dimensional observations.
icml-2007-hierarchical-gaussian-process-.tldr: Hierarchical Gaussian process latent variable models represent conditional independencies alongside manifold structure and are applied to visualizing human motion.

paragraphs: Mixtures of tree-structured distributions provide a way to model relationships among multiple variables using several relatively simple components. Finite versions have already been found efficient and effective. This paper extends the approach with a Dirichlet process, allowing a countable collection of possible tree-structured components instead of fixing a finite component count in advance.

The Bayesian formulation addresses the question of how many components to use by computing a posterior distribution over that number. It also uses Bayesian model averaging to integrate out components. This makes uncertainty about mixture complexity part of the modeling process, rather than requiring the analysis to rely on a single selected number of components.

The authors apply the framework to historical climate archives to identify predominant precipitation patterns. The application concerns both how many major patterns are present and what their properties are. It illustrates why uncertainty over component count matters: identifying recurring structures in multivariate observations involves learning their complexity as well as their individual characteristics.
icml-2007-infinite-mixtures-of-trees-c52.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture of tree distributions treats component count probabilistically and is applied to discovering predominant precipitation patterns.

paragraphs: Partial least squares builds directions that are useful for predicting outputs. Its kernel version combines this iterative construction with a learning runtime described as sub-cubic. The paper examines what changes when PLS is kernelized, with attention to properties that do not occur in ordinary PLS and to their implications for understanding the algorithm.

The analysis develops connections between kernel PLS, kernel ridge regression, and conjugate gradient descent. It also addresses degrees of freedom, a way of describing the flexibility of the fitted model. The authors show how to define this quantity correctly for kernel PLS and efficiently compute an unbiased estimate of it.

These theoretical contributions are tied to the practical task of selecting a model. The paper demonstrates effective model selection using the degrees-of-freedom estimate and discusses efficient cross-validation implementations. Its significance is that understanding the method's structure leads to tools for choosing model complexity, alongside a clearer account of how kernel PLS relates to other learning and optimization procedures.
icml-2007-kernelizing-pls-degrees-of-fre.tldr: The paper analyzes kernel PLS, derives an efficiently computed unbiased degrees-of-freedom estimate, and uses it for effective model selection.

paragraphs: Large-scale kernel learning can require solving a dense positive definite linear system. This creates a computational challenge because the system lacks the sparsity that might otherwise simplify its solution. The paper focuses on the numerical procedure used for this step, a concern directly relevant to large-scale regularized least-squares classification.

Existing work emphasized fast matrix-vector multiplication combined with conjugate gradient iteration. The authors propose using domain decomposition to solve the system instead. They interpret the approach through von Neumann's alternating projection framework, providing a way to understand both its convergence properties and its speed.

The reported applications to machine-learning problems show significant and consistent improvements in convergence speed over conjugate gradient. The stated gain is therefore about reaching a solution more quickly in the evaluated problems. The broader contribution is to bring a different solver strategy into large-scale kernel learning and connect its observed computational behavior with an established framework for analyzing repeated projections.
icml-2007-large-scale-rlsc-learning-with.tldr: A domain decomposition solver yields significant, consistent convergence-speed improvements over conjugate gradient in the reported kernel-learning applications.

paragraphs: Feature selection often begins by treating every feature as equally likely to matter. This paper learns a more informative starting point from related prediction tasks. Its central assumption is that features have descriptive meta-features that predict their relevance, and that the tasks share a similar structure governing which features are useful.

The method models relevance as a function of these meta-features, controlled by shared hyperparameters called meta-priors. A convex optimization algorithm jointly learns the meta-priors and task feature weights. What transfers between tasks is knowledge about feature relevance, making the approach applicable even when tasks use nonoverlapping features or individual features have different relevance across tasks.

This matters because transferable knowledge need not depend on matching the same input coordinates everywhere. The paper demonstrates improved performance on two real datasets: predicting ratings in collaborative filtering and distinguishing the arguments of verbs in sentences. These applications illustrate the stated settings where sharing relevance information can help despite differences in the features used by individual tasks.
icml-2007-learning-a-meta-level-prior-fo.tldr: Learning shared priors from feature meta-features improves prediction across related tasks, including tasks with different or nonoverlapping features.

paragraphs: Kernel learning determines a representation of similarity that can guide downstream learning. Many approaches restrict this representation to a chosen parametric family or a linear combination of predefined kernel matrices. The paper argues that these restrictions reduce flexibility when the observed data contain diverse patterns that the chosen forms may not fit well.

The proposed method learns a nonparametric kernel matrix from pairwise constraints. Its key challenge is maintaining a connection between this flexible matrix and the original input patterns. The authors address that by using the observed data's graph Laplacian as a regularizer. They formulate the optimization as semidefinite programs and provide an efficient algorithm for solving the resulting problem.

The regularizer supplies data-based structure while the pairwise constraints guide the learned similarities. This allows the approach to avoid the specified parametric restrictions without disconnecting the kernel from the inputs. Extensive evaluations on clustering with pairwise constraints find it more effective than other state-of-the-art kernel-learning techniques in the comparisons reported.
icml-2007-learning-nonparametric-kernel-.tldr: Graph Laplacian regularization links a nonparametric kernel matrix to observed inputs, improving constrained clustering in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Paired observations can share statistical structure while also containing variation specific to each dataset. The paper introduces a mixture of probabilistic canonical correlation analyzers to study those relationships locally. It extends canonical correlation analysis beyond a single global linear account of the dependencies between the paired data.

The mixture formulation permits different kinds of observations to exhibit different dependency patterns. A full Bayesian treatment supports analysis when samples are few relative to the number of variables, a setting highlighted as important in bioinformatics. It also enables rigorous estimation of the degree of dependence and independence, making uncertainty about the relationship part of the analysis.

A further extension separates shared variation from variation specific to one dataset. Together, these features let the model address where dependencies occur, how strongly they are supported, and which variation is not shared. The contribution is a modeling framework that combines local dependency structure, small-sample analysis, and a decomposition of the sources of variation in cooccurring observations.
icml-2007-local-dependent-components-cb4.tldr: A Bayesian mixture of canonical correlation models captures local dependencies and separates shared from dataset-specific variation in paired observations.

paragraphs: Regression data can have different noise levels at different inputs. The paper develops a Gaussian process model for this situation, known as heteroscedastic regression. It uses one Gaussian process for the underlying noise-free output and a second for the noise variance, allowing the amount of uncertainty due to noise to vary across the input space.

The main change concerns how the noise variance is inferred. Instead of approximating its posterior with Markov chain Monte Carlo, the method uses a most likely noise approach. The resulting model is described as easy to implement and directly compatible with existing extensions of standard Gaussian processes, including sparse approximations.

This compatibility matters because modeling variable noise can then be combined with other established GP capabilities. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, including a challenging robotics perception problem. The findings support the proposed inference approach as a practical way to use a separate noise model within Gaussian process regression.
icml-2007-most-likely-heteroscedastic-ga.tldr: A most likely noise approach makes Gaussian process regression with input-dependent noise straightforward to implement and compatible with standard GP extensions.

paragraphs: Neighbor search supports tasks such as classification and retrieval, but efficient search structures do not necessarily account for the overall geometry of the dataset. Graph-based semi-supervised methods can capture that geometry, yet the paper identifies scalability and parameter tuning as obstacles. It proposes a neighbor-search method that incorporates global geometry without requiring parameter tuning.

The authors introduce deterministic walks as a counterpart to Markov random walks. This leads to using minimax distance as the measure of dissimilarity. The important shift is that neighbor relationships reflect the dataset's global structure, rather than relying only on a search procedure that overlooks that structure.

To make the distance useful computationally, the paper develops a message-passing algorithm with linear time and space scaling. Empirical studies in image retrieval and semi-supervised learning show useful behavior. The contribution thus joins a geometrically informed definition of neighbors with an efficient calculation procedure, addressing the practical cost of bringing global structure into neighbor search.
icml-2007-neighbor-search-with-global-ge.tldr: A parameter-free neighbor-search method incorporates global geometry through minimax distance computed by a message-passing algorithm with linear time and space scaling.

paragraphs: When monitoring a spatial phenomenon, observations can be scheduled in advance or chosen sequentially using earlier measurements. The paper asks when the adaptive strategy offers a significant advantage. For Gaussian process models, it develops a theoretical bound quantifying the performance difference between active observation selection and a design fixed beforehand.

The approach considers unknown kernel parameters and balances two purposes for collecting observations. Exploration reduces uncertainty about those parameters. Exploitation selects observations near-optimally when the parameters are known approximately. The strategy is nonmyopic, treating observation choices in terms of their broader role in learning and sensing rather than only their immediate payoff.

The authors examine several exploration strategies and provide logarithmic sample-complexity bounds for the exploration phase. They also extend the algorithm to nonstationary Gaussian processes by using local model structure, and evaluate it extensively on real-world problems. The work links the question of whether adaptation helps with algorithms that explicitly manage the uncertainty responsible for that potential advantage.
icml-2007-nonmyopic-active-learning-of-g.tldr: The paper bounds the benefit of adaptive Gaussian process sensing and develops algorithms balancing parameter exploration with informed observation selection.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a regularization procedure for sparse Bayesian classification. Its focus is on making the choice of regularization coefficients computationally efficient while retaining effective classification. The method works with the Hessian of the log-likelihood, the matrix describing how the likelihood's curvature changes across parameter directions.

The authors transform that matrix into diagonal form and regularize its eigenvector directions. This permits explicit optimization of the evidence as a product of one-dimensional integrals. Under the proposed procedure, automatic determination of the regularization coefficients converges in one iteration. That statement concerns this coefficient-selection process, rather than saying that every part of classifier training requires only one step.

The paper develops versions using Gaussian and Laplace priors. Both are reported to deliver performance comparable to state-of-the-art relevance vector machines while taking less training time. They also produce sparser decision rules when sparsity is measured in degrees of freedom. The stated result combines computational savings with reduced model flexibility and comparable predictive performance.
icml-2007-on-one-method-of-non-diagonal-.tldr: Regularizing Hessian eigenvector directions enables one-iteration coefficient selection and yields faster, sparser classifiers with performance comparable to relevance vector machines.

paragraphs: The paper studies matrix update rules derived from relative entropy minimization, concentrating on an online principal component analysis algorithm. These rules update density matrices using a softmin calculation involving matrix logarithms and exponentials. The main contribution is to show that this family of updates can be kernelized.

Kernelization matters here because it connects the update procedure with a feature representation whose dimension affects the theoretical bounds. The authors emphasize that the provable bounds depend logarithmically on feature dimension. This dependence comes with an explicit condition: feature vectors must have their Euclidean norm bounded by a constant.

The central application is therefore an online kernel PCA method built from these entropy-motivated matrix updates. The result links a particular style of matrix optimization to kernel-based learning while preserving the relevance of its dimension-dependent analysis. Its stated significance is theoretical and algorithmic: it makes kernelization available for this update family and explains why the associated bounds are attractive under the bounded-feature assumption.
icml-2007-online-kernel-pca-with-entropi.tldr: Entropy-based matrix updates can be kernelized for online PCA, with bounds logarithmic in feature dimension when feature norms are bounded.

paragraphs: The paper presents a way to learn parameters in relational Bayesian networks by turning the model's likelihood calculation into a computation graph. The likelihood measures how well parameter choices account for the observed data. Expressing that calculation as a graph provides the computational structure needed to optimize it.

The algorithm uses this likelihood graph to carry out gradient ascent, adjusting parameters in directions that increase likelihood. Its applicability rests on a specific requirement: all combining rules in the network must be differentiable. Within that condition, the method includes non-decomposable rules, weighted combinations, and rules nested inside other rules.

This scope matters because the approach can accommodate several complex forms of relational combination within a common optimization procedure. The authors explore its feasibility using artificial random graph data, considering both complete and incomplete observations. Those experiments provide evidence about whether the computational approach can be used in these settings, complementing the stated characterization of which relational models it supports.
icml-2007-parameter-learning-for-relatio.tldr: Compiling relational Bayesian networks into likelihood computation graphs enables gradient-based parameter learning whenever their combining rules are differentiable.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a quadratically gated mixture of experts for nonlinear classification with multiple classes. It addresses incomplete data, where only some of an example's values are observed. The central modeling question is how to learn a classifier while also accounting for the unobserved parts of its inputs.

The authors show that handling missing values entails jointly estimating the data manifold and the classifier. This allows imputation to adapt during classifier learning, connecting estimates of missing values with the evolving model. They derive an expectation-maximization algorithm to maximize the joint likelihood, with the adaptive imputation calculated analytically during the expectation step.

The importance of the joint formulation is that learning the structure of the data and learning class predictions participate in the same estimation procedure. The method is evaluated on three benchmark datasets, where it produces significant improvements over competing methods. These results support the proposed combination of nonlinear classification and adaptive missing-value estimation in the tested settings.
icml-2007-quadratically-gated-mixture-of.tldr: A quadratically gated mixture of experts jointly learns a classifier and data structure, adapting missing-value estimates and improving results on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to generate synthetic networks that resemble a large observed graph. The desired similarities include its degree distribution, small diameter, and spectrum. It proposes Kronecker graphs as a model that naturally exhibits these properties, together with a fitting algorithm called KronFit.

The main computational challenge is fitting the generator to a real network. A naive fitting approach would require super-exponential time. KronFit exploits the structure of the Kronecker product and uses sampling to achieve linear-time fitting. This makes estimating a graph-generation model practical at a scale where the naive approach would be prohibitively expensive.

Experiments on large real and synthetic graphs show that the fitted models closely reproduce patterns in the target graphs. The result supports using a compact generative description to capture important network properties. The authors identify anonymization, extrapolation, and graph summarization as possible uses of the fitted parameters and generated networks; these are applications of the model rather than separate guarantees established by matching graph patterns.
icml-2007-scalable-modeling-of-real-grap.tldr: KronFit fits Kronecker graph models in linear time and reproduces important patterns of large target networks in experiments.

paragraphs: Classification scores are often interpreted as confidence, but the paper questions that interpretation for support vector machines because it lacks a theoretical justification. When uncertainty matters, the authors favor estimating conditional class probabilities. They focus particularly on ambiguity near the decision boundary, where examples are difficult to assign confidently to one class.

The proposed method adapts maximum likelihood estimation within logistic regression. It produces proper conditional probabilities within an interval chosen by the user, accepting lower precision outside that interval. This concentrates the model's probability-estimation effort in the region of interest instead of demanding the same precision everywhere.

The resulting classifier is also sparse: only a small number of training examples contribute to the solution. The paper reports improved computational efficiency relative to logistic regression. Preliminary experiments show improvements over standard logistic regression and performance similar to support vector machines. Together, these findings suggest a way to combine focused uncertainty estimation with a compact classifier, while retaining the explicitly limited probability precision outside the selected interval.
icml-2007-sparse-probabilistic-classifie.tldr: A sparse logistic-regression adaptation estimates class probabilities precisely within a user-selected interval while improving computational efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper introduces statistical predicate invention as the task of discovering new concepts, properties, and relations in structured data. It brings together hidden-variable discovery in statistical modeling and predicate invention in inductive logic programming. The goal is to learn useful relational concepts rather than rely entirely on a vocabulary supplied beforehand.

The proposed initial model uses second-order Markov logic, allowing both predicates and their arguments to be variables while leaving the domain incompletely specified in advance. Its learning procedure repeatedly refines clusters of symbols using the clusters of symbols with which they occur. For example, relations can be grouped according to the groups of objects they connect.

The model permits multiple overlapping ways of clustering because different groupings may better predict different subsets of relational statements. This gives concept discovery flexibility beyond a single partition of the symbols. On several relational datasets, the approach outperforms Markov logic structure learning and the infinite relational model, supporting the usefulness of the proposed discovery mechanism in those evaluations.
icml-2007-statistical-predicate-inventio.tldr: A second-order Markov logic approach discovers relational concepts through multiple interacting clusterings and outperforms two established approaches on several datasets.

paragraphs: Large classification datasets can be reduced by clustering examples before training. The Support Cluster Machine develops a classifier around that setup, using the resulting clusters as its training inputs. Its purpose is to reduce computational cost while still allowing predictions for individual examples at test time.

The key ingredient is a compatible kernel that measures similarity both between two clusters and between a cluster and an individual vector. These two capabilities connect cluster-based training with ordinary example-based prediction. The paper also proves that the method is a general extension of the support vector machine with a radial basis function kernel.

Experiments report substantially lower computational costs for both training and testing, with comparable classification accuracy. This supports the cluster representation as an effective way to handle the evaluated large-scale problems. The authors additionally describe the approach as promising for privacy-preserving data mining. That is a potential application of working with clusters, rather than a stated guarantee that clustering alone establishes privacy.
icml-2007-support-cluster-machine-e932f3.tldr: The Support Cluster Machine trains on clusters through a compatible kernel, substantially reducing training and testing costs while retaining comparable accuracy in experiments.
